description: A low-resource Windows browser shell built on WebView2, whose core bet is that hibernated is a tab's default state and live is a budgeted exception.
consumer_notes: This file is the authoritative machine-readable model of WHY this codebase is shaped the way it is. Source code records what the system does; this graph records the reasoning, the rejected alternatives, and the constraints that must not be violated. Agents should read this before proposing architectural changes. Every node has a stable `id` that is safe to reference in commits, issues, and other documents. When you add a feature, add its nodes/edges here in the same commit.

node_types.problem: An observed user-facing or system-level problem the project exists to solve.
node_types.concept: A domain idea or mental model used to reason about the system.
node_types.decision: An architectural choice that was actively made, with alternatives that were rejected.
node_types.constraint: A hard limit imposed by a platform, API, licence, or law of physics. Cannot be designed away.
node_types.component: A concrete code artifact (class, module, file) in this repository.
node_types.api: An external platform API the design depends on.
node_types.metric: A measurable quantity used to validate the design.
node_types.commit: A unit of work in this repository's history.

edge_types.constrains: Source limits the design space of target.

nodes.label: Users hoard tabs and will not close them
nodes.summary: People keep 100-500 tabs open because the tab strip is the only place where 'things I still care about' remain visible. Refusing to close is a rational response to untrustworthy retrieval, not user error.

nodes.label: The RAM cost of tabs is invisible to users
nodes.summary: Users experience the symptom (a slow machine) but do not attribute it to the browser. Because the cost is never made legible, there is no pressure to change behaviour.

nodes.label: Existing tab suspenders restore lossily
nodes.summary: Chrome Memory Saver, The Great Suspender and similar tools lose scroll position, form state and media timestamps on restore. The papercut causes users to disable the feature, so the memory is never actually reclaimed.

nodes.label: Tab archivers become graveyards
nodes.summary: OneTab, Session Buddy and Toby convert a visible anxious pile into an invisible list nobody revisits. Users intuit this and resist adoption, correctly.

nodes.label: Per-renderer baseline dominates browser memory
nodes.summary: A Chromium renderer costs roughly 40-80 MB for a blank page (V8 isolate, Blink, Mojo, sandbox) before any content loads. At 100 tabs that is ~6 GB of pure overhead. Tab COUNT, not page weight, is the primary cost driver.
nodes.implication: Any memory strategy that does not reduce the number of live renderers is treating a symptom.

nodes.label: A tab strip holds five different data types
nodes.summary: Active work, a todo, a reference doc, a read-later item, and a fear-of-loss artifact all wear the same UI costume. Applying one lifecycle policy to all five is why every existing tool fails.

nodes.label: Refindability score
nodes.summary: How hard a tab would be to recover if closed. A homepage or Wikipedia article is trivially refindable; a filtered dashboard view, a deep search result, or a half-filled form is not. Aggressive eviction is acceptable only for trivially refindable tabs.

nodes.label: Trade RAM for disk (measured ~8,000:1)
nodes.summary: A hibernated tab costs a screenshot plus serialised state on disk, versus tens to hundreds of MB of RAM live.
nodes.predicted: ~150 KB per snapshot, ~200:1 against a 40-80 MB tab.
nodes.measured_0004: 26.8 KB average per PNG snapshot across 7 real sites (188 KB total). Marginal cost of one live tab measured at roughly 230 MB on the same workload, giving a real trade nearer 8,000:1 -- around forty times better than predicted. PNG was expected to be the wasteful choice; page screenshots compress well because large areas are flat colour.
nodes.implication: Disk cost is effectively free at any realistic tab count. 1,000 hibernated tabs would occupy roughly 27 MB. There is no reason to ration snapshots or downscale them for space.

nodes.label: Hibernated is the default state, live is the exception
nodes.summary: Every other browser treats loaded as default and unloading as an emergency. Chrome Memory Saver and Firefox tab unloading are REACTIVE, triggering only under memory pressure. Hearth inverts this: tabs are documents on disk that get temporarily instantiated, under a hard budget.

nodes.label: Build a shell on WebView2 rather than fork an engine
nodes.summary: WebView2 provides the modern web for free and natively exposes the exact primitives this architecture needs: TrySuspend/Resume, CapturePreview, and MemoryUsageTargetLevel. A Gecko fork would give deeper process-model control but costs months before the UX thesis can be tested at all.
nodes.rationale: De-risk the product thesis on the cheap substrate first. If screenshot-backed restore does not feel convincing here, a Gecko fork inherits the same failure.
nodes.revisit_if: Shell-level control proves insufficient to hold a hard memory ceiling, or cross-platform support becomes a requirement.

nodes.label: C# / .NET 9 / WPF as the host framework
nodes.summary: WPF is the most mature WebView2 host, builds from the CLI without MSIX packaging friction, and allows direct control over individual CoreWebView2Controller lifetimes.
nodes.rationale: Chosen partly by environment: .NET 9 SDK and VS 2022 present, no Rust toolchain installed. WinUI3 was rejected for packaging friction.

nodes.label: One shared CoreWebView2Environment for all tabs
nodes.summary: Every WebView2 created from a single environment shares ONE browser process. Allowing each control to create its own environment (the default) spawns a browser process per tab and destroys the memory budget before it exists.
nodes.rationale: This is the single highest-leverage line of code in the project.
nodes.invariant: Never call EnsureCoreWebView2Async without passing the shared environment.

nodes.label: No per-tab memory API is exposed
nodes.summary: Neither WebView2 nor Chromium exposes per-renderer memory to embedders. Per-tab cost must be inferred by measuring the reclaim delta across a suspend/resume cycle, or by attributing OS process working sets.
nodes.workaround: Measure system-wide working set of the WebView2 process tree before and after eviction; attribute the delta to the evicted tab. Self-calibrating over time.

nodes.label: Widevine DRM requires a licence agreement
nodes.summary: Netflix, Spotify and Prime need Widevine. WebView2 inherits Edge's Widevine support, but a shipped product needs a licence relationship with Google. Not a coding problem.

nodes.label: WebView2 is Windows-only in practice
nodes.summary: WebView2 targets Windows. Cross-platform would require CEF, Tauri's wry, or a per-OS webview abstraction.

nodes.label: CapturePreview requires a live, realised WebView2
nodes.summary: A screenshot can only be taken while the WebView2 still exists and has rendered. The capture must therefore happen at tab-BLUR, immediately before eviction, never after.
nodes.implication: A tab restored from a cold session has no screenshot until it has been live once.
nodes.violated_in_0004: The first implementation captured inside HibernateAsync, which runs AFTER ActivateAsync has already collapsed the outgoing tab. A collapsed controller has nothing to photograph, so every capture produced a 0-byte file. Fixed by capturing the outgoing tab in ActivateAsync before any visibility change. Recorded because the constraint was written down first and still got violated -- the correct place to capture is not where eviction happens, it is where focus leaves.
nodes.corollary: Never write a captured file directly from the capture stream. A failed capture leaves a 0-byte PNG that is indistinguishable from a real snapshot at the call site, and would license a teardown that cannot be repainted. Buffer in memory and only write on non-zero length.

nodes.label: Renderer count exceeds tab count because of site isolation
nodes.summary: WebView2 inherits Chromium site isolation, which allocates a renderer per site instance INCLUDING cross-origin iframes. Measured at commit 0002: 5 tabs (example.com, wikipedia, HN, github, stackoverflow) produced 14 renderer processes and 1170 MB total working set, roughly 234 MB per tab.
nodes.implication: A shared environment guarantees one BROWSER process, not one renderer per tab. Capping live tabs alone does not cap renderers; ad-heavy or widget-heavy pages fan out. This makes eviction MORE valuable than the original 40-80 MB per-tab estimate implied, not less.
nodes.known_lever: RETRACTED in 0003. --renderer-process-limit was assumed to be the lever; it is not. See k.no-process-model-control.
nodes.tradeoff: Moot â€” the lever does not exist. Site isolation cannot be traded away from the embedder side at all.

nodes.label: An embedder has NO control over the WebView2 process model
nodes.summary: Chromium process-model switches passed via AdditionalBrowserArguments reach the browser process and are then ignored. Measured at 0003 on stackoverflow.com with 1 live tab: no flags = 14 renderers / 1179.9 MB; --renderer-process-limit=4 = 14 / 1164.4; --process-per-site = 14 / 1170.9; both = 14 / 1161.2. The flag was verified present in the browser process command line, so this is not a plumbing bug.
nodes.implication: Renderer count is a function of page content alone. The ONLY memory lever available to a WebView2 embedder is reducing the number of live tabs -- i.e. eviction. This validates c.hibernate-by-default by elimination: it is not merely the best approach on this substrate, it is the only one.
nodes.informs_v2: A Gecko fork regains this control, since dom.ipc.processCount genuinely caps the content-process pool. This is now the strongest single argument for d.webview2-shell being a staging post rather than the destination.
nodes.resolved_indirectly_in: 0005 — see d.content-blocking-is-the-indirect-lever. The process model stays untouchable, but renderer count is a function of page CONTENT, and content is something an embedder controls absolutely. Refusing cross-origin subframes achieved what every Chromium switch failed to do.

nodes.label: Control renderer count through content, not through the process model
nodes.summary: Since no process-model API is available, low-power mode refuses cross-origin subframe documents and media at the WebResourceRequested filter instead. Renderer count is downstream of what the page is allowed to load, so declining the fan-out sources achieves the cap directly.
nodes.measured_0005: One tab on stackoverflow.com: normal = 14 renderers / 1355.6 MB; low power with blocking = 1 renderer / 301.0 MB (-78%); low power with blocking DISABLED = 14 renderers / 1242.8 MB. The third run is the control that matters -- it isolates the reduction to frame blocking rather than to the tighter budget, which with a single tab never binds at all.
nodes.rationale: This is the answer to k.no-process-model-control and it closes the loop opened in 0003. Every Chromium switch was ignored; a content filter moved renderer count from 14 to 1.
nodes.revisit_if: WebView2 ever exposes real process-pooling, at which point capping directly would be preferable to breaking pages.

nodes.label: Blocking cross-origin frames breaks real functionality
nodes.summary: Refusing cross-origin subframes removes embedded video players, OAuth and SSO login flows, comment widgets, payment frames, CAPTCHAs and map embeds. These are not incidental -- some are the only route through a page.
nodes.implication: Through 0007 this is why it was a MODE and not a default. Since 0008 it IS the default, which is only defensible because d.filtering-needs-an-escape-hatch gives a user who hits a broken login both an explanation and a one-click remedy in the same place.

nodes.label: Reduce live tabs; do not attempt to tune the process model
nodes.summary: Following k.no-process-model-control, Hearth spends no further effort on Chromium switches. RendererProcessLimit and ProcessPerSite remain in HearthOptions but default to OFF, retained as documented dead ends so they are not rediscovered and retried.
nodes.rationale: Measured: eviction alone cut memory 35% (TrySuspend) to 66% (full teardown) at a fixed 8-tab workload, while every process-model flag produced no change whatsoever.
nodes.revisit_if: WebView2 exposes a supported process-pooling API, or the project moves to a substrate whose process model the embedder can actually configure.

nodes.label: Full teardown is the real lever; TrySuspend is a half-measure
nodes.summary: At budget=3 over the same 8-site workload, TrySuspend reclaimed 35% (1823 -> 1188 MB) while destroying the controller reclaimed 53% (1823 -> 854 MB). Suspension retains the controller and therefore a large share of the cost.
nodes.rationale: TrySuspend is worth keeping as the fast-resume tier for recently-blurred tabs, but it cannot carry the memory promise on its own.
nodes.status: ON by default since 0004, gated on holding a snapshot. TabManager falls back to suspension whenever no snapshot exists for a tab, so the reclaim is taken in the common case without ever evicting a page that cannot be repainted.
nodes.reconfirmed_0004: On a corrected harness (one build, 95s settle) suspension reclaimed 32% and teardown 49% against the same 8-tab baseline, preserving the ordering established in 0003.

nodes.label: CoreWebView2EnvironmentOptions.AdditionalBrowserArguments
nodes.summary: Passes raw Chromium command-line switches to the browser process at environment-creation time. The only route to process-model control from an embedder, and therefore the only lever on k.site-isolation-multiplies-renderers.

nodes.label: CoreWebView2.TrySuspend()
nodes.summary: Suspends a WebView2, freeing significant renderer memory while keeping the controller alive for fast resume. Requires the controller to be invisible first. This is hibernation tier 1.

nodes.label: CoreWebView2.CapturePreviewAsync()
nodes.summary: Captures the visible content of a WebView2 to a PNG or JPEG stream. Used to produce the visual placeholder that makes an evicted tab indistinguishable from a live one.

nodes.label: CoreWebView2.MemoryUsageTargetLevel
nodes.summary: Hints to the runtime that a WebView2 should minimise memory usage. Cheaper and lower-fidelity than TrySuspend; usable as an intermediate tier for recently-blurred tabs.

nodes.label: Steady-state working set at high tab count
nodes.summary: Target: total working set stays flat as tab count grows. Reference points: Chrome at 100 tabs is 6-10 GB, Firefox 2-4 GB. Hearth target is under 1.5 GB regardless of tab count.

retracted_0002_interpretation.claim_made: 5 tabs cost 1170 MB, roughly 234 MB per tab, extrapolating to over 20 GB at 100 tabs.
retracted_0002_interpretation.why_it_was_wrong: Only the LAST startup URL was activated, so that run had 1 live tab, not 5. The 14 renderers and 1170 MB belonged to stackoverflow.com's cross-origin frames alone. Page complexity was misread as per-tab cost.
retracted_0002_interpretation.disproof_0003: 1x stackoverflow = 14 renderers / 1176.9 MB. 5x stackoverflow = 14 renderers / 1166.6 MB. Identical. Cold tabs cost nothing, which the architecture predicted but 0002 failed to actually test.
retracted_0002_interpretation.lesson: Always report LIVE tab count alongside open tab count. They are different numbers and conflating them invents cost that does not exist.

measured_0003.method: 8 real sites, every tab activated in turn via HEARTH_ACTIVATE_ALL, working set summed over the WebView2 process tree filtered to Hearth's own user-data-dir.

measured_0004.method: Corrected harness: ONE build, 95s settle, only the teardown flag varied. Supersedes measured_0003, which sampled at 40s before the activation sequence had finished loading all 8 tabs and therefore compared partially-loaded runs.
measured_0004.note: The baseline is higher than 0003's (2234 vs 1823 MB) because every tab now fully loads before sampling. Reduction percentages hold their shape, and the deepest budget improved from 66% to 72%. Conclusions from 0003 are unchanged; only the numbers are now trustworthy.
measured_0004.harness_fix: HEARTH_FULL_TEARDOWN was previously settable only to ON, making it impossible to A/B against its own absence on a single build. Now bidirectional. A flag that cannot be turned off cannot be measured.

flatness_0003.method: budget=3, full teardown, tab count varied.
flatness_0003.interpretation: Memory is decoupled from tab count. 16 tabs cost LESS than 4 because the residual variance is driven by which pages happen to be live at the end, not how many tabs exist. This is the core thesis validated.

nodes.label: Restore fidelity
nodes.summary: Whether a rehydrated tab returns to the same scroll offset, form state and media position. The product thesis fails if users can feel eviction happening.
nodes.done_0004: Screenshot placeholder painted during rebuild, and scroll offset captured at blur and replayed on NavigationCompleted. 7 of 7 blur events produced valid captures across 8 real sites.
nodes.still_missing: Form field values, sessionStorage, media currentTime, and per-scroll-container offsets (only window scroll is restored). A torn-down tab still performs a real network reload, so restore is not instant -- the placeholder hides the rebuild rather than removing it.
nodes.unverified: Still unconfirmed by a human that the swap from placeholder to live content is imperceptible. The 220 ms guess is gone as of 0012: the placeholder now waits for HasRendered, the signal NavigationCompleted already sets, capped at five seconds.
nodes.done_0012: Placeholder is paint-driven rather than timer-driven, dissolves over 200 ms instead of cutting, and fills the pane (UniformToFill) instead of letterboxing.

nodes.label: Memory reclaimed per eviction
nodes.summary: Working-set bytes returned to the OS by evicting one tab. Doubles as the per-tab cost estimate that makes the invisible cost legible to users.

nodes.label: App / StoreRoot
nodes.summary: Application entry point. Owns StoreRoot, the single on-disk location for the WebView2 user-data folder, hibernation screenshots and the session index.

nodes.label: MainWindow
nodes.summary: Application shell. At commit 0001 it hosts a single WebView2 and creates the shared environment, proving the toolchain. Becomes the tab-strip host in later commits.

nodes.label: TabState
nodes.summary: Four-state lifecycle enum (Live, Warm, Hibernated, Cold). Ordered so that a higher value means cheaper to hold and slower to restore; eviction always moves a tab to a higher value.

nodes.label: BrowserTab
nodes.summary: A tab's durable identity: URL, title, activation history. Deliberately NOT a WebView2 wrapper â€” the View property is nullable and null is the expected steady state. Carries LastActivatedUtc and ActivationCount to drive eviction ordering.
nodes.invariant: Null View must never be treated as an error condition. Tabs are documents; renderers are a cache.

nodes.label: TabManager
nodes.summary: Owns tab lifetime and the single shared CoreWebView2Environment. Holds the environment as a Task awaited by every realisation, so tabs share one initialisation instead of racing to create their own.
nodes.invariant: RealiseAsync is the ONLY place permitted to call EnsureCoreWebView2Async, and it always passes the shared environment.

nodes.label: 0001 - scaffold
nodes.summary: Repo initialised, WPF + WebView2 shell builds and navigates, documentation and knowledge-graph structure established.

nodes.label: 0002 - tab model
nodes.summary: Tab abstraction and TabManager introduced; environment ownership moved out of the window. Verified one browser process across 5 tabs, and discovered site isolation multiplies renderers well beyond tab count. NOTE: its per-tab cost interpretation was retracted in 0003.

nodes.label: 0003 - live budget and eviction
nodes.summary: Live-tab budget with score-based eviction. Established that no Chromium process-model flag has any effect through WebView2, that eviction is therefore the only lever, and that under a fixed budget memory is fully decoupled from tab count. Retracts 0002's per-tab cost claim.

nodes.label: Every colour is a DynamicResource token, never a literal
nodes.summary: Light and Dark are two dictionaries with an identical key set, swapped in place at slot 0 of the merged dictionaries. Nothing in the app names a colour directly, so a theme change repaints the whole window without rebuilding any visual tree.
nodes.rationale: Neutrals are Apple's system greys, requested explicitly. The accent darkens from #E8833A to #C25E14 in light rather than being reused: ember on white fails contrast and reads washed out. A light theme is not an inverted dark theme.
nodes.invariant: Both dictionaries must expose exactly the same keys. A key present in one and missing from the other resolves to nothing after a swap and paints transparent. Converters must resolve brushes per call rather than caching them, or a swap applies only half-way.
nodes.revisit_if: A third theme is needed, at which point the key set should be generated rather than hand-maintained.

nodes.label: Custom-chrome windows maximise over the taskbar
nodes.summary: A WindowStyle=None window maximises to full monitor bounds rather than the work area, covering the taskbar and swallowing whatever sits at the bottom of the layout. Windows asks only once, via WM_GETMINMAXINFO, so the work area has to be supplied in the answer rather than corrected afterwards.
nodes.implication: Removing the native title bar is not free. The first build hid the memory readout behind the taskbar whenever the window was maximised -- the readout that exists specifically to make cost visible.
nodes.workaround: MaximiseFix hooks WM_GETMINMAXINFO and resolves the monitor per-window rather than assuming the primary, so it stays correct on multi-monitor setups.

nodes.label: PowerShell 5.1 round-trips corrupt non-ASCII source
nodes.summary: Get-Content in Windows PowerShell 5.1 decodes BOM-less UTF-8 as ANSI. Reading a source file and writing it back re-encodes every non-ASCII character: an em dash becomes three bytes of mojibake, a middle dot becomes 'A-with-circumflex plus dot'.
nodes.implication: This shipped a visible UI bug -- the Big Picture subtitle rendered as '6 open A. one stays awake'. A blanket Latin-1 to UTF-8 repair then made it worse, because the file held a MIX of correct and doubly-encoded text and box-drawing characters degraded to replacement characters.
nodes.rule: Edit source with the file-editing tools, never with a PowerShell read-modify-write. Where a C# file must carry punctuation, define it as a named constant so there is one place to check. Keep comment separators ASCII.
nodes.superseded_by: k.non-ascii-literals-do-not-survive-tooling. The rule here named one bad tool; it was followed, and the characters were lost anyway by a different mechanism in 0008.

nodes.label: Leaving Big Picture puts everything else to sleep immediately
nodes.summary: Exiting the wall calls HibernateAllButActiveAsync, evicting every tab except the one just chosen, regardless of budget headroom.
nodes.rationale: Leaving the wall is the clearest signal available that the user surveyed everything and picked one thing. Waiting for some later activation to push tabs past the ceiling would be reactive eviction, which is precisely the behaviour c.hibernate-by-default exists to reject.
nodes.synergy: Combined with Big Picture pinning the budget to 1, the wall is both the cheapest state to sit in and the moment the rest of the session goes cold.

nodes.label: ThemeManager
nodes.summary: Swaps the token dictionary at runtime and follows the Windows theme via AppsUseLightTheme, watching UserPreferenceChanged. An explicit user choice is never overridden by the OS.
nodes.invariant: The token dictionary is always slot 0 of MergedDictionaries; it is replaced in place so styles declared after it keep resolving.

nodes.label: MaximiseFix
nodes.summary: Hooks WM_GETMINMAXINFO so a custom-chrome window maximises to the work area instead of over the taskbar. Resolves the monitor per-window for multi-monitor correctness.

nodes.label: 0007 - UI overhaul
nodes.summary: Native title bar removed and the tab strip became the caption; full light/dark token theming following Windows; animated hover, selection and mode transitions; Big Picture reworked into true fullscreen with lifting cards; exiting it now hibernates everything else.

nodes.label: WebView2 paints above all WPF content, regardless of Z-order
nodes.summary: The WPF WebView2 is a windowed HWND control hosted through HwndHost. Windows composites it above the WPF render surface, so Panel.ZIndex, overlays and adorners have no effect against it. Discovered at 0006: the Big Picture overlay was correctly built and completely invisible behind a live page.
nodes.implication: Any full-window UI in this app must COLLAPSE the WebView2 host rather than stack above it. There is no Z-order fix.
nodes.silver_lining: For Big Picture this is not a workaround but the honest design: the mode shows a wall of pictures, so no live page needs to be on screen at all.
nodes.consequence_0010: Collapsing the host is not free: a WebView2 cannot finish initialising inside a collapsed panel, which is k.collapsed-host-blocks-initialisation.

nodes.label: A tab blurred before first paint photographs blank
nodes.summary: CapturePreviewAsync succeeds on a realised-but-unpainted WebView2 and returns a blank frame. ActivateAsync returns once the renderer exists, not once the document has loaded, so a fast tab switch captures nothing useful.
nodes.implication: Capture is gated on BrowserTab.HasRendered, set from a successful NavigationCompleted and cleared on teardown. A refused capture correctly also withholds permission to tear the tab down, since there would be nothing to repaint from.
nodes.why_it_matters: A blank thumbnail reads as a broken page rather than an unvisited one, which is worse than showing no thumbnail at all.
nodes.harness_note: This also invalidated the HEARTH_ACTIVATE_ALL benchmark, which switched tabs faster than any page could load. It now dwells until each tab has painted -- a harness that switches instantly measures a workload nobody has.

nodes.label: Big Picture pins the live budget to one
nodes.summary: Entering the full-screen tab wall forces EffectiveBudget to 1. You are looking at a wall of pictures, so exactly one page needs to be real.
nodes.rationale: The lean-back aesthetic and the memory architecture want the same thing here, which is the reason the mode is worth having rather than being a skin. Steam Big Picture shows one game at a time; Hearth shows one page, with everything else as the screenshots hibernation was already producing.
nodes.synergy: The snapshots that make tabs cheap are the same artifacts that make them findable. The overview costs nothing extra because eviction already paid for it.

nodes.label: SnapshotConverter
nodes.summary: Loads tab snapshots for the Big Picture wall, decoding at 480px wide. Paths carry a '?t=ticks' suffix so bindings invalidate on re-capture, since the file path alone is stable and would never signal a change.
nodes.rationale: Decoding full-resolution page captures for dozens of thumbnails would spend more memory on the tab overview than on the tabs, which would be an absurd way to lose the argument.

nodes.label: 0006 - Big Picture mode
nodes.summary: Full-screen, keyboard-driven wall of tab snapshots with the live budget pinned to one. Discovered the WPF airspace constraint and the blank-capture-before-first-paint bug.

nodes.label: MemoryProbe
nodes.summary: Samples the working set of Hearth's own process tree via a Toolhelp32 snapshot, walking descendants of the current PID. Makes the memory readout in the taskbar a measured figure rather than an estimate.
nodes.rationale: Descendants are walked rather than filtering every msedgewebview2.exe on the machine, because Windows runs several other WebView2 apps (Widgets, Store, Teams) whose memory is not ours to report.
nodes.invariant: Never display a memory number this process has not actually observed. The project's argument is that the cost is real; a fabricated figure forfeits it.

nodes.label: 0005 - taskbar and low-power mode
nodes.summary: Replaced the developer status strip with a real taskbar: navigation, a measured memory readout in plain language, and a low-power toggle. Low power tightens the budget and refuses cross-origin frames and media, cutting stackoverflow.com from 14 renderers to 1.

nodes.label: SnapshotStore
nodes.summary: Captures and persists a tab's last painted frame plus its scroll offset, and replays the offset on rehydrate. This is what makes teardown survivable: an evicted tab renders its own last frame rather than going blank.
nodes.invariant: Capture only ever happens at blur, on the outgoing tab, before any visibility change. Never write the capture stream straight to a file -- buffer it and check for non-zero length first.

nodes.label: 0004 - screenshot-backed hibernation
nodes.summary: Snapshot capture at blur, scroll replay on restore, placeholder painting during rebuild, and teardown enabled by default gated on holding a snapshot. Also corrected the measurement harness and re-measured; 0003's figures were sampled before runs had settled.

nodes.label: HearthOptions
nodes.summary: All memory tunables in one record, with environment-variable overrides so configurations can be A/B tested from a script without rebuilding. Gathered deliberately: 'you set a RAM ceiling and the browser respects it' cannot be delivered by values scattered through the codebase.

nodes.label: EvictionPolicy
nodes.summary: Scores live tabs worst-first. Recency decays as 1/(1+idleMinutes) and is weighted by log(1+activationCount), so a reference doc reopened twenty times outranks an article opened once and abandoned. Never-activated tabs score negative infinity and are evicted first.
nodes.future: This is where c.refindability lands: a filtered dashboard view or half-filled form must resist eviction far harder than a homepage, because being wrong costs a loss rather than a reload.

nodes.label: Keyboard input reaches the shell by two separate paths, and WPF alone is deaf
nodes.summary: WebView2 is out-of-process: the HWND holding keyboard focus is created by msedgewebview2.exe, so its WM_KEYDOWN messages queue to THAT process's thread. Window.PreviewKeyDown therefore never fires while a page has focus, and no thread-level message filter can help either -- there is no message on our thread to filter. Page keys arrive only via CoreWebView2Controller.AcceleratorKeyPressed.
nodes.implication: Any keyboard feature must be wired on BOTH paths and resolve through one shared map, or it will work in the address bar and silently do nothing on a page.
nodes.why_it_hid: After startup, focus sits on the address bar. Every manual test that pressed a key without first clicking into the page exercised the one path that already worked.
nodes.invariant: ShortcutRouter.Map is static and pure, and is the only place a key becomes a command.

nodes.label: The WPF WebView2 wrapper does not expose CoreWebView2Controller
nodes.summary: Microsoft.Web.WebView2.Wpf.WebView2 surfaces CoreWebView2 but not the controller that owns AcceleratorKeyPressed, ZoomFactorChanged bounds and visibility. The controller lives on a private field m_webview2Base, whose CoreWebView2Controller property is internal. Verified by reflecting over the pinned 1.0.4078.44 assembly.
nodes.implication: Page-level keyboard handling requires reflection. It is cached once per process and fail-soft: a failed lookup degrades shortcuts to chrome-only and logs, rather than throwing at startup.
nodes.risk: This is the only place in the codebase reaching into SDK internals. It is why the WebView2 package version is pinned rather than floating, and it is checked at startup so a break is visible instead of silent.

nodes.label: Both keyboard paths fire for the same keystroke
nodes.summary: With the native hook attached, a key pressed on a page is delivered twice: the WPF wrapper re-raises it into the WPF tree AND the controller reports it natively, about 4 ms apart. Measured directly -- one Ctrl+T opened two tabs.
nodes.implication: The chrome path must decline any keystroke that originated in web content, but only while the native hook is known to be working.
nodes.the_trap: IsKeyboardFocusWithin reports False and Keyboard.FocusedElement is null while a page holds focus. Neither is a bug -- WPF genuinely does not have focus -- which is precisely why neither can be used to detect that it does not. e.OriginalSource is the WebView2 and is the only reliable discriminator.

nodes.label: CoreWebView2.Source is still about:blank when a tab's first request goes out
nodes.summary: WebResourceRequested for the top-level document fires before the navigation commits, so Source has not yet become the target URL. Any 'is this request same-origin with the current page' test written against Source therefore refuses the page's own navigation.
nodes.implication: This shipped in 0005 and was invisible for three commits, because filtering could only be engaged mid-session -- by which time a page had committed and Source was real. Making it the default surfaced it as a blank page on every tab.
nodes.lesson: A bug that only appears when a feature becomes the default was always there; being a mode was hiding it. Moving anything to on-by-default is a re-test of everything it touches, not a config change.

nodes.label: Browsing runs lean by default; there is no low-power toggle
nodes.summary: The live budget is 3 and content filtering is on from startup, with no mode control in the chrome. What used to be 'low power' is simply what the browser is; immersion (0009) is the opposite pole, entered deliberately and at a measured cost.
nodes.rationale: c.hibernate-by-default says hibernated is a tab's default state. A browser that only honours that once the user finds a toggle does not hold the thesis -- it offers it. The product promise is a RAM ceiling respected by construction, and a ceiling that ships switched off is not a ceiling.
nodes.supersedes_reasoning: 0005 made this a mode because blocking breaks logins with no recourse. That reasoning was correct and is not being dismissed: it is answered by d.filtering-needs-an-escape-hatch, which is the per-site allowlist 0005 itself recorded as the way out.
nodes.revisit_if: Users are found clicking the shield on most sites they visit. That would mean the default is wrong rather than merely strict, and the honest response is a looser default filter, not a louder shield.

nodes.label: A default that breaks pages must announce itself and be overridable in one click
nodes.summary: SiteRules holds a persistent per-host allowlist. The tab counts refused requests, the shield appears in the address bar only when the count is non-zero, and one click exempts the host permanently and reloads.
nodes.rationale: Filtering can only be a default if a user who hits a broken login has an explanation and a remedy in the same place. A permanently visible badge is wallpaper; one that appears exactly when a button stops responding is the explanation needed at that moment. Cost of the hatch is one click per site, paid once. Cost of not having it is the whole feature being switched off.
nodes.measured_0008: Granting stackoverflow.com took the page from 1 renderer back to 14, and the status bar from 719 MB to 1.6 GB. Making that jump visible is the point, not a side effect.
nodes.revisit_if: Grants need scoping ('just this once', or per-frame rather than per-host), or a UI to review and revoke them. Today the only way to revoke is to delete store/site-rules.json.

nodes.label: Classify requests with Sec-Fetch headers, not by comparing URLs
nodes.summary: The content filter reads Sec-Fetch-Dest (what the request is for) and Sec-Fetch-Site (how far it reaches) rather than inferring a request's role from its URL against the tab's current one. dest=document is never refused; dest=iframe with site=cross-site is.
nodes.rationale: Chromium computes these on every request and they depend on no state the embedder has to keep correct. The URL-comparison version needed Source to be current, and k.source-is-stale-during-navigation says it is not. Asking the engine what a request IS removes a whole class of ordering bug rather than fixing one instance of it.
nodes.side_effect: The rewrite narrowed media blocking to cross-site only. Same-origin media costs no extra renderer -- 0005's control run located the win in frames -- so refusing a page's own audio player broke sites in exchange for nothing.
nodes.revisit_if: A request needs blocking that carries no Sec-Fetch headers. A host-comparison fallback against tab.Url is retained for exactly that case.

nodes.label: ShortcutRouter
nodes.summary: One key map served down two delivery paths: HandleWpfKey for chrome focus and Attach for page focus. Reaches CoreWebView2Controller by cached, fail-soft reflection, reads modifiers from the OS rather than from WPF, and declines chrome-path keys that originated in web content.
nodes.invariant: Map is static and pure. Both paths must resolve through it; a second key-to-command table anywhere is a bug.

nodes.label: SiteRules
nodes.summary: Persistent per-host allowlist at store/site-rules.json. Hosts are normalised with www stripped so one grant covers what a user considers one site. A corrupt file costs the exemptions, never the launch.
nodes.rationale: This is the component that makes filtering-by-default defensible rather than merely aggressive.

nodes.label: Diag
nodes.summary: Opt-in trace log at store/trace.log, enabled by HEARTH_TRACE=1. Off by default; tracing never throws.
nodes.rationale: 0008's central claim -- that a keystroke landing on a page reaches the shell -- cannot be checked by reading code or looking at the window, because both paths look identical from outside and the failure mode is silence. This is the instrument that makes the keyboard claim measurable rather than asserted.

nodes.label: Memory reclaimed by content filtering, as a default
nodes.summary: One tab on stackoverflow.com, one Debug build, 90 s settle, only HEARTH_BLOCK_FRAMES varying. Filtering on: 1 renderer / 719 MB. Filtering off (control): 14 renderers / 1599 MB, a 55% reduction. Granting the site via the shield returns it to 14 renderers / 1.6 GB.
nodes.caveat: Debug build, and the total includes Hearth's own WPF process, so absolute figures are NOT comparable with 0005's 301 MB / 1356 MB. The within-run control is what the claim rests on.
nodes.confirms: Reproduces 0005's 14-to-1 renderer result under the narrower cross-site-only rule, showing the narrowing cost nothing.

nodes.label: 0008 - keyboard and lean default
nodes.summary: Browser keyboard shortcuts wired on both delivery paths and verified through the real OS input stack; low-power toggle removed and lean made the default; per-host allowlist and address-bar shield added; content filter rewritten onto Sec-Fetch headers after it was found blocking top-level navigations.

nodes.label: Chromium switches can only be set when the browser process starts
nodes.summary: AdditionalBrowserArguments is read once, by CoreWebView2Environment.CreateAsync, and never again. WebView2 additionally refuses to create a second environment over the same user-data folder with different options while the first browser process is alive.
nodes.implication: Any setting expressed as a Chromium switch cannot be changed in a running process. This is why switching modes RESTARTS Hearth rather than reconfiguring it -- the alternative was a mode that claims to boost performance while changing nothing that matters.
nodes.corollary: The outgoing process must fully exit before the new one can create its environment, so the replacement is passed --handover=<pid> and waits.

nodes.label: A maximised window never gets the taskbar to hide, whatever size it is
nodes.summary: Setting WindowState.Maximized and answering WM_GETMINMAXINFO with full monitor bounds produces a window measuring exactly 1920x1080 at 0,0 -- confirmed through every WebView2 child HWND and in WPF's own layout -- and the shell still draws the taskbar on top of it. To Windows, a maximised window is by definition one that respects the work area.
nodes.implication: Real fullscreen is WindowState.Normal, Topmost, sized explicitly to the monitor in DIPs. MaximiseFix.Fullscreen does this; the WM_GETMINMAXINFO hook is only for browse mode.
nodes.lesson: Two wrong fixes preceded the right one, both from reasoning about the symptom. Enumerating the child HWNDs settled it in one step by showing the app had been correct all along and the shell was declining to yield.
nodes.gotcha: Monitor bounds are physical pixels and Left/Top/Width/Height are DIPs. Skipping the conversion looks correct at 100% scaling and leaves a strip of desktop showing everywhere else.

nodes.label: Mouse input over web content never reaches WPF, and has no native escape hatch
nodes.summary: The window under the cursor belongs to msedgewebview2.exe, so MouseMove, MouseDown and PreviewMouseDown on the host stay silent while the pointer is over a page -- the same out-of-process delivery as k.two-keyboard-paths. Unlike the keyboard there is NO AcceleratorKeyPressed equivalent for the mouse.
nodes.implication: Pointer gestures can only be recognised inside the page, by an injected listener posting through window.chrome.webview.
nodes.known_limit: Injection cannot work where page script cannot run: the PDF viewer, browser error pages, downloads, view-source. Every gesture therefore needs a keyboard equivalent, which goes down the native key path instead.

nodes.label: Changing mode relaunches the process
nodes.summary: Immersion and browse differ in Chromium switches, so switching writes the session, starts a new process with --mode= and --handover=, and exits. The new instance waits for the old one to release the user-data folder before creating its environment.
nodes.rationale: Forced by k.browser-args-fixed-at-creation. The honest alternative was not 'switch modes live' -- that is unavailable -- but 'ship a mode that changes nothing measurable'. A restart that visibly reconfigures the engine is better than a toggle that lies.
nodes.cost: About two seconds and a window flash. Paid down by cmp.sessionstore, which makes the restart lossless for tab identity.
nodes.revisit_if: WebView2 ever allows per-controller switches or a live environment swap. Then immersion becomes a live transition and the session save becomes a pure safety net.

nodes.label: The session file persists tab ids, not just URLs
nodes.summary: store/session.json carries each tab's Guid. On restore the tab is rebuilt with the same id and SnapshotStore.Adopt re-attaches the screenshot already sitting at store/shots/{id}.png.
nodes.rationale: Snapshots are keyed by tab id. Restoring with fresh ids would orphan every screenshot the previous run captured -- still on disk, permanently unreachable -- and the grid would come back blank after every restart, which is exactly when a wall of thumbnails is most useful.
nodes.honesty: Adopt restores the IMAGE only. The scroll offset was captured in a process that has exited and was never persisted, so it is deliberately left at zero rather than faked. Restored tabs are cold: reopening 40 tabs must cost 40 URLs, not 40 renderers.
nodes.revisit_if: Scroll offsets get persisted alongside the image, at which point restore fidelity across restarts becomes a claim worth making.

nodes.label: Immersion evicts by pure recency; browse keeps habit weighting
nodes.summary: EvictionOrder takes a recencyOnly flag. Immersion orders strictly by LastActivatedUtc so the last few tabs in the chain stay warm. Leaving the grid in immersion also does not hibernate the rest, which browse does.
nodes.rationale: 'The last few in the chain' is a different question from 'what is worth keeping'. Habit weighting is right for a working session -- a reference doc opened forty times should outrank something opened once -- but in a lean-back session it keeps the dashboard checked every morning alive instead of the thing being watched two tabs ago.
nodes.synergy: Evicting recent tabs every time the grid closes would make the grid the most expensive thing in the mode it exists to serve.

nodes.label: HearthMode / ModeProfile
nodes.summary: The two poles and everything that differs between them: live budget, content filtering, eviction ordering, and the Chromium switches. Browse deliberately carries no switches so it remains a valid control condition for every published memory number.
nodes.invariant: Mode is fixed for the lifetime of the process. Anything that wants to vary it must go through App.RestartInto.

nodes.label: SessionStore
nodes.summary: Persists tabs to store/session.json across restarts, written atomically via a temp file and a move. Consumed and deleted on load, so a crash during restore cannot loop the browser into reopening the tabs that caused it.
nodes.rationale: Exists to make d.mode-switch-restarts affordable. A browser that loses your tabs when you change a setting is one nobody changes the setting on.

nodes.label: GestureScript
nodes.summary: The listener injected into every page and frame. Both-buttons-and-swipe changes tabs; thumb buttons navigate. Both-down is e.buttons & 3 === 3, a chord no page uses, which is why it can be claimed without breaking sites. The context menu is suppressed only for a completed swipe.
nodes.rationale: The only place a pointer gesture can be recognised, per k.mouse-input-never-reaches-wpf.

nodes.label: What immersion costs against browse
nodes.summary: Six real sites, every tab activated so the budget binds, one Debug build, 95 s settle. Browse: 3 renderers / 890 MB. Immersion: 20 renderers / 2197 MB -- about 2.5x.
nodes.why_it_belongs_next_to_the_feature: The thesis is not that memory does not matter. It is that the user should decide when to spend it and be able to see what they spent. A mode whose cost is unpublished is the same invisible-cost problem the project exists to attack (p.invisible-cost).

nodes.label: 0009 - immersion mode
nodes.summary: Immersion added as the opposite pole to browse: real device fullscreen, generous recency-chain budget, filtering off, GPU and anti-throttling Chromium switches. Switching modes relaunches the process because those switches are fixed at environment creation, which required session persistence. Both-buttons swipe and thumb-button navigation added via injected script.

nodes.label: A WebView2 cannot finish initialising inside a collapsed panel
nodes.summary: EnsureCoreWebView2Async waits for a realised HWND. A Visibility.Collapsed WPF element does not have one, so the call never returns -- it does not fail, it hangs.
nodes.implication: Any UI that collapses the content host for airspace reasons (k.wpf-airspace) MUST restore it before activating a tab. TabManager holds the budget semaphore across activation, so one hung call wedges every later one too.
nodes.why_it_looked_intermittent: Big Picture pins the live budget to 1, so nearly every card in it is a COLD tab and needs a new renderer. Picking a tab that still held a controller took the early-return path in RealiseAsync and worked perfectly. The failure rate was a function of which card you clicked.
nodes.invariant: MainWindow.RestoreShell runs, including a forced UpdateLayout, before any activation triggered from the grid.

nodes.label: The grid takes the shape the app is already in, and never resizes the window
nodes.summary: The grid spans rows 1-3 rather than the whole window and never touches WindowState. In browse the tab strip stays visible above it and it fills the window at whatever size that is; in immersion the strip is already collapsed, so the same markup fills the screen.
nodes.rationale: One layout, two correct results, and no mode check in the XAML. Up to 0009 the grid forced the window to maximise, so opening it resized the browser and leaving it did not reliably put the window back -- a tab switcher should not be a window manager.
nodes.detail: The tab strip doubles as the title bar, so collapsing it in browse would take the window controls with it. The subtitle does differ per mode, because the guarantee differs: 'one stays awake' versus 'the last few stay awake'.
nodes.revisit_if: The grid needs to be usable at very small window sizes, where the tab strip plus header may leave too little room for a single row of cards.

nodes.label: One click opens a card; numbers 1-9 jump straight to one
nodes.summary: The grid opened on MouseDoubleClick until 0010. A single click selected a card and appeared to do nothing at all.
nodes.rationale: This was the single biggest reason the grid read as broken. Nothing else in this app, and no tab switcher anyone has used, needs two clicks to pick a thing. In a wall of pictures the position is the identity, so a number key is the most direct thing a keyboard can offer alongside it.
nodes.cost: There is no click target left for selecting a card without opening it, so per-card actions -- close, pin -- will need their own hit areas rather than a selection state.

nodes.label: Opening flies a copy of the card up to fill the viewport
nodes.summary: A VisualBrush copy of the chosen card is painted onto a Canvas spanning every row and animated to cover the viewport, while the rest of the wall fades underneath it.
nodes.rationale: The transition should make the page you land on visibly the card you chose. A cut, or a plain crossfade, leaves the user to re-establish where they are.
nodes.why_a_copy: The card cannot be animated in place: it lives inside the ListBox's ScrollViewer, which clips to its bounds, so it would be sliced off exactly as the movement got interesting.
nodes.why_cover_not_fit: A letterboxed intermediate frame gives away that this is a thumbnail and not the page.
nodes.safety: Falls back to a plain fade when the container has been virtualised away or laid out at zero size. A decorative animation must never be able to block the actual open.

nodes.label: 0010 - tab grid
nodes.summary: Found and fixed the reason picking a tab from the grid hung: activation was started while the content host was still collapsed. Grid no longer resizes the window and inherits the current mode's shape; single click and number keys open a card; opening zooms the card into the page; the ListBox now scrolls itself instead of sitting inside an outer ScrollViewer.

nodes.label: The address bar tracks the active tab, not keyboard focus
nodes.summary: Sync overwrites the address bar whenever the active tab changed, even while the field has focus. It only preserves in-progress text when the tab is the same one the text belongs to.
nodes.rationale: Guarding on focus alone was wrong because focus SURVIVES a tab switch: Ctrl+T focuses the bar, and every switch after that (Ctrl+Tab, Ctrl+1, Ctrl+Shift+T, picking a card) happened while it still had focus. The bar then displayed the previous tab's URL over the current tab's page.
nodes.why_it_matters: The address bar is the only place the interface states what you are looking at, and every judgement a person makes about whether to trust a page starts there. A browser that misreports the current URL is not a cosmetic problem.
nodes.discovered_in: 0011, in the 0010 flow test: strip highlighted Example Domain, page was example.com, bar read en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tab_interface.

nodes.label: 0011 - address bar follows the tab
nodes.summary: The address bar no longer keeps showing the previous tab's URL after a switch made while it had keyboard focus.

nodes.label: A non-ASCII literal in source must survive every tool that touches the file, and will not
nodes.summary: This source has lost non-ASCII content twice by unrelated mechanisms. In 0007 a PowerShell round-trip re-encoded it, because PS 5.1 reads BOM-less UTF-8 as ANSI. In 0008 a read-then-rewrite dropped the private-use-area glyphs entirely, because tools that display source render them as nothing, so they came back as empty strings.
nodes.discovered_in: 0012 (the second instance; 0007 recorded the first as k.powershell-utf8-corruption)
nodes.shipped: The maximise/restore caption button and the immersion button were both empty strings from 0008 to 0012. The file compiled and the window simply had no restore control.
nodes.why_the_old_rule_was_not_enough: 0007's rule named one bad tool -- do not round-trip through PowerShell -- and that rule WAS followed. The hazard is not a specific tool, it is depending on a byte sequence surviving a chain of them, including merely reading the file.
nodes.rule: Write every non-ASCII character in C# source as a \uXXXX escape. Escapes are pure ASCII on disk so nothing can drop them, and they state the code point rather than relying on a glyph rendering. MainWindow.xaml.cs is verified to contain zero bytes above 0x7F. XAML may use &#xNNNN; entities, which are ASCII for the same reason.
nodes.invariant: Every hand-written C# file under src/Hearth contains zero bytes above 0x7F. Checkable in one line: sum(1 for b in open(path,"rb").read() if b > 127) == 0. An invariant that cannot be checked is a hope, and this one was already violated twice without anyone noticing.
nodes.swept_in_0012: Writing the rule down caught the next instance immediately: 49 further non-ASCII characters in C#, of which 46 em dashes and 2 arrows were in comments and one was in a user-visible string literal -- the ellipsis that truncates tab titles in the strip. That one became an escape; the comment characters became -- and ->.

nodes.label: UI that must appear OVER a live page is a separate top-level window
nodes.summary: EdgeBar is a borderless, non-activating, owned Window rather than an overlay inside MainWindow. Immersion's sliding tab strip, address bar and status readout are hosted in two of them.
nodes.rationale: k.wpf-airspace makes an in-window overlay invisible the moment a page paints. 0006 solved that for the tab grid by collapsing the content host, which works for a full-screen surface and is useless for a toolbar: the entire point is to show controls WITHOUT hiding the page. A sibling HWND composites above the WebView2 child, and the page below never changes size.
nodes.rejected_alternative: Letting the rows reflow to make room. That resizes the WebView2 on every reveal, reflowing the page underneath -- unacceptable in the mode built around watching video.
nodes.details: ShowActivated=false, because an activating window would pull focus out of the page and drop the owner out of the shell's fullscreen treatment, bringing the taskbar back (k.maximised-is-not-fullscreen). The panel slides, not the window, because moving the window forces a redraw of the live page underneath every frame. The real chrome is re-hosted rather than duplicated, so there is one address bar and one memory readout.
nodes.revisit_if: The bars need to work outside immersion, where the owner can move and resize; today bounds are synced only at reveal.

nodes.label: The zoomed card hands off to the placeholder instead of fading out
nodes.summary: Opening from the grid ends the zoom HOLDING the card at full size, puts the same tab's snapshot into the placeholder underneath, and cross-fades the grid away to reveal it. The placeholder then waits for HasRendered rather than a fixed delay.
nodes.rationale: k.collapsed-host-blocks-initialisation forces the order 'animate, then activate', so the zoom finished and the page load began with nothing on screen in between. That gap is what read as clunky; no easing curve fixes a hole. Handing the image off means the picture that flew up to fill the screen is still the picture on screen while the page loads behind it.
nodes.supporting_fixes: Easing moved from 280ms QuarticEase EaseIn (crawls, then snaps) to 360ms CubicEase EaseInOut. Placeholder stretch moved from Uniform/DownOnly/centred, which letterboxed the capture, to UniformToFill top-aligned. An indeterminate bar runs while the placeholder is up, which is exactly the window in which WPF is visible at all.
nodes.replaces_a_guess: The placeholder used to drop on a flat 220 ms timer that 0004 recorded as a guess. It now waits for HasRendered, capped at five seconds so a page that never loads cannot pin a screenshot over itself.

nodes.label: EdgeBar
nodes.summary: A borderless, non-activating, owned top-level window that slides chrome in at the top or bottom edge in immersion. Hosts the real TitleBar/NavBar/StatusBar, lifted out of MainWindow's layout, so nothing is duplicated.
nodes.invariant: Never activates and never resizes the owner. Both would undo the fullscreen state the mode depends on.

nodes.label: 0012 - chrome fixes and immersion edges
nodes.summary: Restored the maximise and immersion buttons, which had been empty strings since 0008, and made every non-ASCII source literal an escape. Labelled the immersion button so it names the restart. Default landing page moved to Google. Grid open transition made continuous via a snapshot handoff and a paint-driven placeholder. Immersion gained pointer-proximity chrome at the top and bottom edges, hosted in separate windows because airspace forbids overlays.

nodes.label: Four durations and four easings, named for purpose, used everywhere
nodes.summary: MotionQuick/Base/Slow/Grand and EaseEnter/Exit/Travel/Emphasis are declared once in App.xaml and mirrored in Motion.cs for code. Every animated control resolves through them.
nodes.rationale: Before 0013 there were two durations and four easings applied more or less at random, and half the controls had no motion at all. The app read as jerky not because any single animation was wrong but because nothing agreed with anything else. Naming by purpose rather than by milliseconds is what stops the set growing again.
nodes.why_duplicated_in_code: Motion.cs restates the values rather than resolving them from the resource dictionary. A mistyped resource key fails silently and leaves an animation that never plays; a mistyped field does not compile.
nodes.revisit_if: A reduced-motion preference is added, at which point every duration needs to collapse to zero from one place.

nodes.label: Animating Opacity on a large subtree forces offscreen composition every frame
nodes.summary: Opacity below 1 on a container with overlapping children makes WPF render that subtree into an intermediate surface each frame. Only Transform, and Opacity on leaf elements, are genuinely cheap.
nodes.measured: Fading the whole tab grid versus fading its scrim, header and footer as separate leaves: long frames per 450 ms entrance fell from 1.0 to 0.7 and the rate rose from about 69 to about 79 fps.
nodes.implication: Corrects the rule written earlier in the same commit, which claimed Opacity and Transform were equally free. Compose entrances out of leaf fades plus a container transform.
nodes.invariant: No animation targets Opacity on a container that has more than a couple of overlapping children.

nodes.label: A WPF Effect is recomputed every frame it is visible
nodes.summary: DropShadowEffect and friends are not cached. A blurred card re-blurs on every frame of any animation touching it, and the cost multiplies by the number of such elements on screen.
nodes.measured: Tab grid entrance, same build, only the effect varying, cold sample discarded: with DropShadowEffect 56/60/62/54/59 fps (mean 58); without 103/115/94/112/115 fps (mean 108). Non-overlapping ranges.
nodes.implication: Elevation is expressed with a hairline border and background contrast instead. Effects are acceptable only on things that do not animate and do not appear in quantity.

nodes.label: Caching a visual to a bitmap before scaling it costs MORE than re-rendering it
nodes.summary: Flying a frozen RenderTargetBitmap of the tab card, rather than a live VisualBrush, cost three times the CPU: 47 ms against 16 ms across the zoom, same build, only the implementation varying.
nodes.why: The rasterisation is not the expense -- it completes before the animation starts. The expense is resampling: a 308px card grown to fill the viewport is a roughly fourfold upscale on every frame. A VisualBrush re-renders vectors and text AT the drawn size, which is cheaper AND sharper; the bitmap goes soft exactly when the card is largest.
nodes.implication: The obvious 'rasterise once' optimisation is wrong for anything that scales up substantially. Reverted; the VisualBrush is the shipped path.
nodes.lesson: This was implemented, justified in a comment, and committed to before being measured. The measurement reversed it.

nodes.label: Setting Timeline.BeginTime to null disables the animation silently
nodes.summary: BeginTime is a TimeSpan? whose default is TimeSpan.Zero. Assigning null does not mean 'no delay', it means the timeline never begins. No error is raised and the animated property simply keeps its declared value.
nodes.how_it_showed: A helper passed an optional TimeSpan? straight through, disabling every animation that did not request a stagger. The tab grid opened completely blank, because its Opacity is declared 0 in XAML and the animation meant to raise it never ran.
nodes.rule: Assign BeginTime only when a delay was actually requested. The failure mode is invisible in review: the call site looks correct and a disabled animation leaves a plausible value rather than throwing.

nodes.label: Motion
nodes.summary: The motion vocabulary in code: four durations, four easings, and animation factories. FadeAsync completes when the animation does, so callers do not have to guess a Task.Delay that runs short and reintroduces a visible seam.
nodes.invariant: Only ever targets Opacity or a Transform.

nodes.label: FrameMeter
nodes.summary: Counts composition frames across an animation and reports rate, CPU cost, and the number of frames longer than 25 ms. Only exists when HEARTH_TRACE=1.
nodes.rationale: Smoothness was the one quality claim in the project that had never been measured. Long-frame count is the headline: mean frame rate saturates at the compositor cap and hides stalls, and process CPU time is too noisy in a process that also hosts a browser.

nodes.label: Delivered animation smoothness
nodes.summary: Tab grid entrance after 0013: 0.7 long frames (>25 ms) per 450 ms entrance across six runs, worst gap 17-78 ms, typically 70-120 fps. The animations are longer than before and drop fewer frames than before.
nodes.caveat: Debug build on one machine with a high-refresh display, so absolute rates are not portable. Every claim in 0013 rests on a within-run A/B where only one thing varied.

nodes.label: 0013 - motion rework
nodes.summary: A shared motion vocabulary applied app-wide, with previously static controls animated and press feedback added. Introduced frame instrumentation, which then disproved three assumptions: drop shadows were halving the frame rate, subtree opacity is not free, and caching the zoomed card to a bitmap cost three times the CPU of the VisualBrush it replaced.

nodes.label: The mark is an arch stroke with a banked ember, not a flame
nodes.summary: A thick arch stroke -- the mouth of a hearth -- with one ember glowing on the floor inside it, on a warm near-black tile. Every size rendered independently at 16x and downsampled, rather than one master scaled down.
nodes.rationale: It says hearth rather than fire, which is the actual idea: the product is about banking embers and coming back to them, not about burning. An arch is also a single closed geometric form, so it survives 16px, and it is not a shape another browser uses.
nodes.rejected_flame: What every fast/hot/energy product already uses, so it says nothing, and its silhouette is thin tapering points that turn to mush below about 24px.
nodes.rejected_solid_arch: Read as a tombstone; adding a bright bar for the hearth floor made it a headstone on a plinth. The error was conceptual, not aesthetic -- a hearth is an OPENING, and a filled shape says the opposite.
nodes.detail: The tile is warm near-black so it reads as a dark object against both a light and a dark taskbar rather than dissolving into either.
nodes.revisit_if: A light-mode icon variant is wanted, or the app ships an installer and needs Store-style asset sizes.

nodes.label: make-icon.py
nodes.summary: Generates src/Hearth/Assets/hearth.ico at 16/24/32/48/64/128/256 and the contact sheet in docs/images/icon.png.
nodes.rationale: An icon committed as an opaque binary is one nobody can adjust later. The script is the source of truth, and its header records the two rejected directions so they are not re-tried.
nodes.invariant: Each size is rendered independently at 16x supersample and downsampled with LANCZOS. Scaling a single 256px master down to 16px produces mud.

nodes.label: 0014 - identity
nodes.summary: Real application icon (arch-and-ember mark, generated and reproducible), wired as both ApplicationIcon and Window.Icon, plus assembly metadata and a browser-style window title. The app no longer shows the generic Windows icon or a WebView2 version string in the taskbar.

nodes.label: The hibernation placeholder was never once on screen
nodes.summary: From 0004 to 0014 the shell painted an evicted tab's screenshot while its renderer rebuilt, and cross-faded it out when the page painted. Filmed at ~37 fps, a switch showed the page being left, then a near-black frame, then the new page cutting in. The snapshot was never visible at any point.
nodes.detail: Two stacked causes. ActivateAsync left the OUTGOING page visible for the whole rebuild, so the placeholder sat under a live HWND; then it showed the INCOMING control the instant its renderer existed, a second or more before it had anything to draw, so the placeholder sat under an unpainted one. WebView2 paints over all WPF content whatever its Z-order or opacity (k.wpf-airspace), so the image was never on screen and the cross-fade at the end animated something nobody could see.
nodes.measurement: Pane luminance across a cold-tab switch, budget 1: page left 229, mid-switch 18 and 78 across two runs, page arrived at 236. After the fix the minimum was 229, 185 and 232 with zero intermediate frames.
nodes.invariant: A transition that hides a WebView2 must take the pages off screen BEFORE the rebuild and hold the new control back until its page has painted. There is no cross-fade available: the honest handoff is a cut between two images of the same page.
nodes.why_it_survived: Every part of it is individually correct and the whole thing is invisible by construction. Only photographing the screen mid-transition finds it, which nothing did before 0015.

nodes.label: NavigationCompleted is about a second later than 'there is something to look at'
nodes.summary: CoreWebView2.NavigationCompleted waits for every subresource on the page. Against google.com it fired after the startup curtain's 2.6 s ceiling had already given up, on a page that had been readable for a second.
nodes.detail: DOMContentLoaded is the honest signal for 'the document exists'. BrowserTab now carries both: HasRendered for capture, which needs the strict one because photographing a half-built page produces a thumbnail of scaffolding, and HasContent for anything deciding when to stop covering the screen.
nodes.measurement: Startup curtain went from hitting the 2600 ms ceiling to ending at 1.0-1.6 s, on the page rather than on a timeout.
nodes.detail_reveal: The reveal gate picks between them: with a snapshot up it waits for the strict signal so the live page matches the picture it replaces; with no snapshot it reveals on DOMContentLoaded plus a longer beat, because revealing on the instant it fires showed the renderer's blank white page for a frame or two.

nodes.label: A self-requeueing Loaded-priority callback blanks the page, not the control it belongs to
nodes.summary: The tab marker retried at DispatcherPriority.Loaded whenever its chip had no size yet. In immersion the tab strip lives in an EdgeBar window that is not shown until the pointer reaches the screen edge, so its chips have no size and never will -- the retry ran forever.
nodes.detail: Loaded priority runs inside the layout phase, so the loop kept that phase permanently busy. HwndHost shows the child window it hosts during a settled layout pass, never got one, and the WEB PAGE stayed blank for the life of the process. The failing control was not the one that showed the symptom.
nodes.measurement: Immersion failed 5 starts out of 5. Browse always passed, because its status bar rewrites itself every two seconds and that was enough to let a pass through. Bounded to a single retry: 10 immersion starts out of 10, and 3/3 in each mode on the shipping build.
nodes.invariant: A dispatcher callback that reschedules itself must have a bounded retry count. One that can never succeed does not fail loudly, it starves whatever shares its priority.
nodes.wrong_turns: Bisected through the immersion browser switches, MaximiseFix.Fullscreen, the startup curtain, Visibility.Hidden versus Collapsed, and collapsing the content host instead of the control. All innocent. A mode carve-out disabling the new reveal in immersion was very nearly shipped as a documented limitation.

nodes.label: A WPF window with AllowsTransparency is composited in software
nodes.summary: Per-pixel-alpha (layered) windows bypass the GPU: the whole window is composited on the UI thread every frame. At browser size that halves the frame rate.
nodes.measurement: Three cold starts each, one build, only the curtain's exit path varying. Opaque: 8.0 ms/frame, 124-125 fps, 0/0/0 long frames, worst gap 9-16 ms, ~292 ms CPU. Window-opacity dissolve: 16.2 ms/frame, 56-67 fps, worst gap up to 114 ms, ~771 ms CPU. Half the frame rate and 2.6x the CPU for the same 1320x860 window.
nodes.detail: The cost scales with pixel count, so a 4K display pays more. Measured at 1320x860.
nodes.revisit_if: A composition-based route to a true window fade appears -- DirectComposition or WinUI hosting -- that does not go through a layered window.

nodes.label: Startup is covered by a curtain carrying the mark, held until the first page has parsed
nodes.summary: An opaque owned top-level window over the whole app, from before the environment exists until the active tab reports DOMContentLoaded, then the mark lifts away and the browser frame drops in behind it.
nodes.rationale: Creating a browser process and loading a page takes seconds and used to happen in full view, as an empty grey window that looked hung. The wait is unavoidable; being shown nothing during it is not.
nodes.why_a_window: An overlay inside MainWindow would be punched through by the first page that painted, in the middle of the screen, which is exactly where the mark is (k.wpf-airspace). The grid's answer -- collapse the content host -- is unavailable, because a WebView2 cannot finish initialising inside a collapsed panel and initialising is what the curtain covers.
nodes.timing: Gated on real readiness with a 2.6 s ceiling and a 700 ms floor. A timed splash is wrong in both directions, and a curtain that appears and leaves inside 200 ms reads as a glitch rather than a transition.
nodes.revisit_if: Startup drops below about half a second, at which point the curtain is longer than the thing it covers.

nodes.label: A mode restart raises the same curtain on both sides of the process boundary
nodes.summary: The outgoing process puts the mark up, launches its successor underneath it, and only then exits. The successor raises the same curtain the moment its window exists.
nodes.rationale: Switching mode kills the application and starts another one, which cannot be hidden. The mark is the only thing that can survive the boundary, so it is what carries the continuity.
nodes.measurement: Launching the successor before the exit rather than in the statement after it overlaps its startup with the curtain animation. One build, alternating: the window where neither process is on screen went from 1.15 s and 1.25 s to 0.66 s and 0.75 s.
nodes.detail: Safe because the successor already waits for the handover before creating its environment (k.browser-args-fixed-at-creation), so overlapping costs nothing. AwaitHandover also became asynchronous: it used to block the UI thread, so the incoming window could not paint and a mode switch showed the unpainted white rectangle Windows draws for a hung application.
nodes.revisit_if: Modes stop requiring a restart, which needs AdditionalBrowserArguments to become settable on a live environment.

nodes.label: A rebuilt tab's control is held back until its page has painted
nodes.summary: TabManager hides every page at the start of a rebuild and does not show the incoming control until a shell-supplied gate returns. The gate holds the tab's snapshot, or the app's own ground and the loading bar when there is none.
nodes.rationale: It is the only way the hibernation placeholder is ever on screen (k.the-placeholder-was-never-visible), and it removes the near-black frame that used to sit in the middle of every switch to an evicted tab.
nodes.detail: The gate is awaited OUTSIDE the budget semaphore. It waits for a real page load, and holding that lock for a page load is exactly what made picking a tab from the grid hang in 0010 (k.collapsed-host-blocks-initialisation). If the user moves on while the page loads, the superseded tab does not get shown.
nodes.no_snapshot: Rebuild is gated on the tab having no renderer rather than on a snapshot existing. Activating a never-visited tab used to leave the previous page up for the whole load; showing nothing is better than showing a page the user has just left.
nodes.revisit_if: WebView2 gains a way to composite into WPF, at which point a real cross-fade becomes possible and the hold becomes unnecessary.

nodes.label: Selection in the tab strip is one marker that moves, not a background that lights up
nodes.summary: A single border slides and resizes between chips. The chips no longer paint their own selected state.
nodes.rationale: Two chips fading in opposite directions read as two unrelated events. Browsers that move a single indicator read as continuous, because the eye tracks one object.
nodes.detail: Its WIDTH is animated, a deliberate exception to d.animate-transforms-only: scaling a fixed-width border on X turns its rounded corners into ellipses over the length of the travel. Safe only because the marker lives in a Canvas, which reports no size of its own and gives children infinite space, so re-measuring it cannot change anything above it.
nodes.coalescing: Sync runs on every state change a tab reports and a busy page reports dozens, since each refused subresource bumps the blocked count. Requests are coalesced onto one deferred pass and dropped when the geometry has not moved, or the marker permanently eases toward a position it is already at.
nodes.revisit_if: The strip gains horizontal scrolling that the marker has to track.

nodes.label: Every transition honours Windows' 'show animations' setting; pointer feedback does not
nodes.summary: SystemParameters.ClientAreaAnimation is read once in Motion and collapses every duration to a single tick when off. HEARTH_MOTION=0/1 pins it either way.
nodes.rationale: A browser is exactly the kind of application people turn animations off for: weak hardware, remote desktop, or a vestibular disorder that makes a full-screen zoom genuinely unpleasant. Every other browser honours it. Reading it in one place means a transition added later cannot forget to.
nodes.detail: It deliberately does not cover hover fills and press dips. Those are 70-130 ms, carry no travel, and removing them makes the controls feel broken rather than calm. What it covers is everything that MOVES something across the screen.
nodes.revisit_if: An in-app settings surface exists, at which point this becomes a visible preference rather than an inherited one.

nodes.label: Veil
nodes.summary: The full-window curtain: an opaque, owned, non-activating top-level window carrying the Hearth mark. Used for the startup cover and for the mode-restart handoff.
nodes.rationale: A sibling HWND composites above WebView2, which is the only way to cover a live page without hiding it (d.airspace-needs-a-second-window).
nodes.invariant: Opaque, never AllowsTransparency. A layered window at this size is software-composited and costs half the frame rate (k.layered-windows-are-software-drawn). HEARTH_VEIL=dissolve keeps the transparent variant reachable for comparison.

nodes.label: HearthMark
nodes.summary: The arch-and-ember mark drawn as vector geometry, with a slow breath on the ember's halo while the browser starts.
nodes.rationale: The curtain shows the mark at 118 px and growing, so scaling up a 256 px bitmap would go soft at exactly the moment it is the only thing on screen. The coordinates are the icon generator's, converted to a 100-unit box, so tools/make-icon.py stays the source of the design (d.hearth-mark).
nodes.invariant: The breath is one Opacity on one small leaf: no effect, no layout, no transform. It runs during the busiest moment in the process and its only job is to say the application is alive rather than hung.

nodes.label: 0015 - transitions
nodes.summary: Startup curtain and mode-restart handoff carrying the mark; the hibernation placeholder made visible for the first time since 0004; a travelling tab-strip marker with chip entrance and exit; a hover-expanding square immersion chip; system reduced-motion honoured. Plus the layout-starvation loop that blanked the page in immersion, and a collapsed-controller capture that hung a switch outright.
